title: Classification Metrics II - Precision, Recall, F1
abstract:
Three metrics that answer the question accuracy cannot: which kind of
mistake is the model making? Precision asks how often the model is right when it
says yes; recall asks how many of the real positives it caught; F1 combines them
for when both matter. This document works both of the notes' examples — the spam
filter where false positives are crucial and the cancer screen where false
negatives are — explains why F1 uses the harmonic mean rather than the
arithmetic one, covers the precision–recall tradeoff and the threshold that
controls it, and gives the rule for choosing which metric to optimise.

blocks.t: Why These Exist
From the notes
These help when accuracy doesn't help.

Topic 47 established the problem: accuracy tells you how many predictions
were wrong but never which kind. Two models can have identical accuracy
and be wildly different in value. Precision and recall separate the two error
types so you can optimise the one that matters.
Precision
From the notes: the spam example
Two spam filters with the same accuracy:
\qquad

Which is better? $FP$ for Model 1 $>$ $FP$ for Model 2, and that
is the crucial error here — we want the lowest error in "not spam"
being marked as spam. So we choose Model 2.

\boxed{ \text{Precision}=\frac{TP}{TP+FP} }
 \qquad\text{"If the model says YES, how often is it correct?"}
It is the proportion of predicted positives that are actually positive.

blocks.cap:
The notes' spam example. Both models have the same accuracy, but Model
 1 wrongly sends 300 real emails to the spam folder against Model 2's 16.
 Precision — the metric that counts false positives — separates them:
 $0.25$ versus $0.86$.

blocks.t: Read the denominator

Precision divides by $TP+FP$ — everything the model predicted positive.
So it lives entirely in the "predicted yes" column of the confusion matrix. It
never looks at the positives the model missed. That is recall's job.
Recall
From the notes: the cancer example
\qquad

Here also the accuracies are the same, so we choose by Type 1 or Type 2
error. Here false negative matters over false positive.

\boxed{ \text{Recall}=\frac{TP}{TP+FN} }
 \qquad\text{"Out of all actual YES cases, how many did we catch?"}

It is the proportion of actual positives that are correctly classified.
We select Model 1 here, since $R_A > R_B$.

blocks.cap:
The notes' cancer example. Model 1 misses 200 cancers, Model 2 misses
 500. Recall counts exactly those misses: $0.83$ versus $0.67$.

blocks.t: Recall has other names

Recall is also called sensitivity, the true positive rate
(TPR), and — in information retrieval — simply "recall". TPR is the name
used on the $y$-axis of the ROC curve (Topic 53). All three are the same
quantity.
The Tradeoff
Why you cannot maximise both

Precision and recall are controlled by the same dial — the decision threshold
(Topic 45) — and it moves them in opposite directions.

items:
Lower the threshold: predict positive more often. You catch more
 real positives (recall rises) but also flag more negatives
 (precision falls).

Raise the threshold: predict positive only when very sure.
 Precision rises, recall falls.

blocks.t:
Both are trivially maximisable on their own: predict positive for every
row and recall is 1; predict positive for the single most confident row and
precision is 1. Neither model is useful, which is exactly why a single combined
number is needed.

blocks.cap:
Left: precision and recall as functions of the threshold — they move
 in opposite directions. Middle: the precision–recall curve, the honest summary
 on imbalanced data. Right: the F1 surface, showing why the harmonic mean
 refuses to reward a lopsided model.

blocks.t: F1 Score
From the notes

Tells us how good the model is when both Type 1 and Type 2 errors
matter.
\boxed{ F_1=2\times\frac{\text{Precision}\times\text{Recall}}{\text{Precision}+\text{Recall}} }

$F_1$ is high only when both precision and recall are high, and vice
versa is true.
Why the harmonic mean
$F_1$ is the harmonic mean of $P$ and $R$:

F_1=\frac{2}{\frac1P+\frac1R}
 =2\cdot\frac{PR}{P+R} .
Compare the two means on a deliberately lopsided model:

The arithmetic mean rates rows 1 and 2 almost identically, which is absurd — a
model with 2% recall catches almost nothing. The harmonic mean is dominated by
the smaller of the two values, so it is high only when both are.
That is precisely the notes' point.
$F_\beta$ — when you want to tilt the balance
F_\beta=\left(1+\beta^{2}\right)\frac{P\cdot R}{\beta^{2}P+R}

$\beta>1$ weights recall more ($F_2$ for cancer screening); $\beta<1$ weights
precision more ($F_{0.5}$ for spam). $F_1$ is the symmetric case. Use $F_\beta$
when you can state how much more one error costs, and the explicit cost
matrix (Topic 09) when you can state the actual amounts.
Choosing Which to Optimise

head: Optimise
When
Examples
rows: A false positive is expensive; you act on every positive prediction
Spam filtering, ad targeting, recommending an expensive intervention
A false negative is expensive; missing a case is unacceptable
Cancer screening, fraud detection, safety-critical defect detection
Both errors matter and are roughly comparable
You must catch a stated fraction
"Catch 90% of fraud — minimise the false alarms"
"The team can call 5{,}000 — maximise the hits"

blocks.t: Report the operating point, not just the number

Precision, recall and F1 are all computed at a threshold. Quoting "F1 =
0.72" without saying at what threshold is incomplete — a different threshold on
the same model gives a different number. For a threshold-free summary use the
PR-AUC (average precision), which is the right curve on imbalanced data
because it ignores the true negatives that dominate ROC-AUC (Topic 53).
Code

import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import (precision_score, recall_score, f1_score, fbeta_score,
                             confusion_matrix, precision_recall_curve,
                             average_precision_score, classification_report)
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

# =====================================================================
# 1. THE NOTES' SPAM EXAMPLE -- precision separates the two models
# =====================================================================
#                 sent to spam   not sent
# spam                 TP            FN
# not spam             FP            TN
models = {
    "Model 1": dict(TP=100, FN=170, FP=300, TN=700),
    "Model 2": dict(TP=100, FN=190, FP=16,  TN=700),
}
print(f"{'':9s} {'accuracy':>9s} {'precision':>10s} {'recall':>8s} {'F1':>7s}")
for name, c in models.items():
    acc  = (c["TP"] + c["TN"]) / sum(c.values())
    prec = c["TP"] / (c["TP"] + c["FP"])
    rec  = c["TP"] / (c["TP"] + c["FN"])
    f1   = 2 * prec * rec / (prec + rec)
    print(f"{name:9s} {acc:9.4f} {prec:10.4f} {rec:8.4f} {f1:7.4f}")
# Accuracies are close, but precision is 0.25 vs 0.86.
# A real email in the spam folder is the crucial error -> choose Model 2.

# =====================================================================
# 2. THE NOTES' CANCER EXAMPLE -- recall separates them
# =====================================================================
cancer = {
    "Model 1": dict(TP=1000, FN=200, FP=800, TN=8000),
    "Model 2": dict(TP=1000, FN=500, FP=500, TN=8000),
}
print(f"\n{'':9s} {'accuracy':>9s} {'precision':>10s} {'recall':>8s} {'F1':>7s}")
for name, c in cancer.items():
    acc  = (c["TP"] + c["TN"]) / sum(c.values())
    prec = c["TP"] / (c["TP"] + c["FP"])
    rec  = c["TP"] / (c["TP"] + c["FN"])
    print(f"{name:9s} {acc:9.4f} {prec:10.4f} {rec:8.4f} "
          f"{2*prec*rec/(prec+rec):7.4f}")
# Same accuracy again. Recall is 0.83 vs 0.67 -- Model 1 misses 200 cancers,
# Model 2 misses 500. Choose Model 1.

# =====================================================================
# 3. WHY THE HARMONIC MEAN
# =====================================================================
print(f"\n{'P':>6s} {'R':>6s} {'arithmetic':>12s} {'F1 (harmonic)':>15s}")
for P, R in [(1.00, 0.02), (0.90, 0.30), (0.60, 0.60), (0.75, 0.45), (0.02, 1.00)]:
    print(f"{P:6.2f} {R:6.2f} {(P+R)/2:12.3f} {2*P*R/(P+R):15.3f}")
# The arithmetic mean calls (1.00, 0.02) a 0.51 model. F1 calls it 0.04.
# The harmonic mean is dominated by the SMALLER value.

# F1 is never above the smaller of the two, and never below half of it:
for P, R in [(0.9, 0.1), (0.5, 0.5), (0.8, 0.4)]:
    f = 2*P*R/(P+R)
    print(f"P={P} R={R}: F1={f:.3f}   min={min(P,R):.3f}   "
          f"F1 <= min: {f <= min(P, R) + 1e-12}")

# =====================================================================
# 4. BOTH ARE TRIVIALLY GAMEABLE ALONE
# =====================================================================
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 5000
X = rng.normal(0, 1, (n, 5))
p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(2.2*X[:, 0] + 1.4*X[:, 1] - 2.6)))
y = (rng.random(n) < p).astype(int)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=.3, stratify=y, random_state=0)

always_yes = np.ones_like(y_te)
print(f"\n'always predict positive': recall {recall_score(y_te, always_yes):.4f}  "
      f"precision {precision_score(y_te, always_yes):.4f}  "
      f"F1 {f1_score(y_te, always_yes):.4f}")

mdl = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
probs = mdl.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]
top1 = np.zeros_like(y_te); top1[np.argmax(probs)] = 1
print(f"'only the single most confident': "
      f"recall {recall_score(y_te, top1):.4f}  "
      f"precision {precision_score(y_te, top1, zero_division=0):.4f}  "
      f"F1 {f1_score(y_te, top1):.4f}")
# Perfect recall and perfect precision, each from a useless model.
# F1 rejects both.

# =====================================================================
# 5. THE THRESHOLD IS THE DIAL
# =====================================================================
print(f"\n{'threshold':>10s} {'TP':>5s} {'FP':>5s} {'FN':>5s} "
      f"{'precision':>10s} {'recall':>8s} {'F1':>7s}")
for t in [0.05, 0.15, 0.30, 0.50, 0.70, 0.90]:
    pred = (probs >= t).astype(int)
    tn, fp, fn, tp = confusion_matrix(y_te, pred).ravel()
    print(f"{t:10.2f} {tp:5d} {fp:5d} {fn:5d} "
          f"{precision_score(y_te, pred, zero_division=0):10.4f} "
          f"{recall_score(y_te, pred):8.4f} {f1_score(y_te, pred):7.4f}")
# Precision rises and recall falls as the threshold rises. Same model throughout.

# =====================================================================
# 6. PICK THE THRESHOLD FOR YOUR ACTUAL OBJECTIVE
# =====================================================================
prec, rec, thr = precision_recall_curve(y_te, probs)

# (a) maximise F1
f1s = 2 * prec[:-1] * rec[:-1] / np.maximum(prec[:-1] + rec[:-1], 1e-12)
i = int(np.argmax(f1s))
print(f"\nbest F1 {f1s[i]:.4f} at threshold {thr[i]:.4f} "
      f"(P {prec[i]:.3f}, R {rec[i]:.3f})")

# (b) "catch 90% of the positives -- minimise false alarms"
ok = rec[:-1] >= 0.90
if ok.any():
    j = int(np.argmax(np.where(ok, prec[:-1], -1)))
    print(f"precision @ recall>=0.90: {prec[j]:.4f} at threshold {thr[j]:.4f}")

# (c) "we can only act on 500 cases -- maximise the hits"
K = 500
top = np.argsort(-probs)[:K]
print(f"recall @ top-{K}: {y_te[top].sum() / y_te.sum():.4f}   "
      f"precision @ top-{K}: {y_te[top].mean():.4f}")

# =====================================================================
# 7. F-BETA -- when you can state HOW MUCH more one error costs
# =====================================================================
pred = (probs >= 0.5).astype(int)
print(f"\n{'beta':>6s} {'F-beta':>9s}  emphasis")
for b in [0.5, 1.0, 2.0]:
    emph = "precision" if b < 1 else ("balanced" if b == 1 else "recall")
    print(f"{b:6.1f} {fbeta_score(y_te, pred, beta=b):9.4f}  {emph}")

# =====================================================================
# 8. THRESHOLD-FREE SUMMARIES
# =====================================================================
print(f"\naverage precision (PR-AUC): {average_precision_score(y_te, probs):.4f}")
print(f"baseline (positive rate)  : {y_te.mean():.4f}")
# On imbalanced data PR-AUC is the honest summary: its baseline is the
# positive rate, whereas ROC-AUC's baseline is always 0.5 (Topic 53).

print("\n", classification_report(y_te, pred, digits=3))
# 'support' is the number of true instances per class -- always read it,
# because a metric computed over 12 rows is not a measurement.
Worked Examples
Precision, recall and F1 from one confusion matrix
Using Model B from the previous chapter: TP $=3$, FP $=4$, FN $=2$, TN $=91$.
Step 1 – precision (of the alarms raised, how many were real):
P = \frac{TP}{TP+FP} = \frac{3}{3+4} = \frac{3}{7} \approx 0.429
Step 2 – recall (of the real frauds, how many were caught):
Step 3 – F1 (harmonic mean, so a weak value drags the score down):

Step 4 – the trade-off in action. Lower the threshold so the model flags more transactions: recall rises to $0.8$, but suppose precision falls to $0.30$. F1 becomes $2(0.30)(0.8)/(1.10) = 0.436$, lower than before, so the change is a net loss by this metric. Choose the threshold on the cost of each error, not on accuracy.
Edge case. Model A from the previous chapter has $TP=0$: recall $=0$, and precision is $0/0$, undefined. Libraries return $0$ and warn.
Summary
Everything on one page

items:
These metrics help when accuracy doesn't help — they separate
 the two error types.

$\text{Precision}=\dfrac{TP}{TP+FP}$ — if the model says YES,
 how often is it correct? The proportion of predicted positives that are
 actually positive. Use it when false positives are the crucial
 error, as with a real email marked as spam.

$\text{Recall}=\dfrac{TP}{TP+FN}$ — out of all actual YES cases,
 how many did we catch? The proportion of actual positives correctly
 classified. Use it when false negatives matter, as with a missed
 cancer.

$F_1=2\times\dfrac{P\times R}{P+R}$ — how good the model is when
 both Type 1 and Type 2 errors matter. $F_1$ is high only when
 both precision and recall are high, and vice versa.

It is the harmonic mean, so it is dominated by the smaller value.
 The arithmetic mean would rate $(P{=}1.0,\ R{=}0.02)$ as $0.51$; $F_1$
 rates it $0.04$.

Precision and recall move in opposite directions as the decision
 threshold changes. Each is trivially maximisable alone, which is why a
 combined measure is needed.

$F_\beta$ tilts the balance: $\beta>1$ favours recall, $\beta<1$ favours
 precision.

Always report the threshold; for a threshold-free summary on
 imbalanced data use PR-AUC.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. Define precision and recall, and say when you would prioritise each.

Precision is $TP/(TP+FP)$ — of the cases flagged positive, how many really are.
Recall is $TP/(TP+FN)$ — of the real positives, how many were caught. Prioritise
precision when acting on a false positive is expensive (spam filtering, expensive
interventions); prioritise recall when missing a positive is unacceptable (cancer
screening, fraud, safety defects).
Q. Why is F1 the harmonic mean rather than the arithmetic mean?

Because the arithmetic mean rewards lopsided models. A classifier with precision
1.0 and recall 0.02 catches almost nothing but scores 0.51 arithmetically. The
harmonic mean is dominated by the smaller value and scores it 0.04 — so F1 is
high only when both are high.
Q. How do you increase recall?

Lower the decision threshold, so the model predicts positive more often. This
requires no retraining — but precision will fall, since you are also flagging
more negatives. The whole precision–recall curve is generated by sweeping that
one dial.
Q. A model has recall 1.0. Is it good?

Not necessarily — predicting positive for every row achieves recall 1.0. Check
precision. That is exactly why F1, or a fixed operating point, is reported instead
of either metric alone.
Q. Your stakeholder says "catch 90% of fraud". What metric?

Precision at recall $\ge0.90$. Fix recall at the stated level, then choose the
threshold maximising precision subject to that — which minimises the false alarms
your investigators must work through.
Q. When would you use $F_2$ instead of $F_1$?

When recall is worth more than precision and you can say roughly how much. $F_2$
weights recall four times as heavily, which suits medical screening. If you know
the actual costs, skip $F_\beta$ and optimise expected cost directly.
Q. ROC-AUC or PR-AUC?

PR-AUC on imbalanced data. ROC-AUC's false-positive rate divides by the huge pool
of true negatives, so it can look excellent while precision is terrible. PR-AUC
ignores true negatives entirely, and its baseline is the positive rate rather than
a flat 0.5.
